title: Chief Voss

pages.text:
*The Handbook of Small Truths, Entry 10: Gruff is only kindness wearing a spanner.*

The sound of heavy boots on the grated floor of the pump house was distinct, a rhythmic thud that vibrated through the metal floor and up into Kess’s knees. She looked up from the drone’s chassis, where a smear of grease darkened her thumb, and watched Chief Engineer Bram Voss enter the narrow corridor. He was stocky and pale, with a shaved head and a bushy ginger beard that seemed to bristle independently of his mood. His grey coverall was stained with oil in the shape of old mistakes, and the red wrench badge on his chest caught the amber glow of the wall lamps.

He stopped. He did not stop moving immediately. He simply ceased to advance, his eyes fixed on the device sitting on the workbench between them. The drone was a haphazard assembly of salvaged parts, its propellers still stiff from the test run, its infrared camera lens clouded with a thin film of condensation.

"Who," Voss began, his voice a low rumble that seemed to come from his chest rather than his throat, "built this?"

Lio straightened up, his hands hovering uncertainly over his wrist-mounted tool-tablet. "It’s a calibration unit, Chief. For the thermal mapping project. We’re just checking the spectral response against the..."

"Calibration unit," Voss repeated. The words tasted like rust in his mouth. He stepped closer, his gaze dropping to the small screen attached to the drone’s side, where a rough, pixelated image of a pump housing glowed with an unnatural, bright orange heat signature. "This is a camera. This is a camera that is currently showing me a pump housing that is running forty degrees above spec. And you are standing here, in a restricted zone, with a device that has no serial number, no safety lockout, and a propeller guard made of what appears to be a cut-down grow-light housing."

Kess felt the heat rise in her cheeks, a prickling sensation that started at her neck and spread to her ears. "It’s safe," she said, though her voice came out thinner than she intended. "We checked the torque on the mounts. The battery is isolated. And the thermal reading is real. That housing is leaking coolant."

Voss looked at her. Then he looked at the screen. The orange glow pulsed softly, a steady, rhythmic beat that matched the hum of the pumps behind them. He opened his mouth to deliver what was undoubtedly the standard lecture on unauthorized access, safety protocols, and the severe consequences of playing with machinery you do not understand. But the words died on his lips. He looked at the orange spot, and his expression shifted, the anger draining out of him like water from a cracked tank, replaced by something harder and colder.
pages.image: In the dim, industrial pump house, Chief Voss, a stocky man with a ginger beard and grey coverall, stares intently at a small, makeshift drone on a workbench; its screen displays a bright orange thermal image of a pump housing, while Kess and Lio stand behind it, looking nervous.

pages.text:
Voss did not yell, nor did he threaten to ground them or confiscate the drone. He simply walked over to a heavy steel toolbox, sat down on it with a thud that rattled the bolts on the lid, and rubbed his face with both hands, the gesture slow and deliberate as he wiped away the frustration that had been building in his shoulders for years.

"You found it," he said. It was a confirmation, heavy and final, like the sound of a door locking. "You actually found it."

Kess waited. Pim, who had been crouching near the drone, looked up, his yellow hair-ties bouncing slightly. "Is it bad?" he asked. "Like, really bad?"

Voss looked at the boy, then at Kess, then at Lio. "It has been bad for eleven years, and lately it is worse," he said. "The radiator loop. The glycol. It is leaking. Not a gush, and not a burst pipe, but a slow, steady weep, a few liters a month, maybe less. Enough to drop the rejection capacity by zero point four percent every month now, and enough to shrink our power margin until it is a thread."

He picked up a wrench from the bench, turning it over in his thick fingers, the metal cool and smooth. "Every year, I file the report. Every year, the Council asks for a repair. And every year, it gets postponed. Why? Because there is no proven fix, and because the joint is in a place we cannot reach without risking the whole wing. We are running on fumes, both of them, and we are too afraid to stop the ship to fix the engine."

Lio leaned against the wall, his arms crossed. "Tally told us the margin is three point one percent. It did not say why. It just said the Orchard’s lights are the easiest thing to cut."

"That is because it is the only thing that is easy," Voss said, his voice flat and hard. "And because it is the thing that hurts the least, in the short term. In the long term, it kills the ship. And we have not even started talking about what happens when the margin hits zero."

Kess looked at the drone, at the orange glow that had started it all. "So the numbers are real," she said. "The leak is real. And we cannot fix it from here."

"No," Voss said. "We cannot." He looked at them, and for the first time, his eyes were not angry, but tired. "But you can find it. That is the first step. The second step is a lot harder."
pages.image: Chief Voss sits on a steel toolbox in the pump house, rubbing his face with his hands, looking exhausted; Kess, Lio, and Pim stand around him, the drone's screen glowing faintly orange in the background, the mood heavy with realization.

pages.text:
Voss’s voice dropped into the careful, measured register of a man explaining the layout of a beehive to a child who had already been stung. "The joint is in the manifold, third segment of the primary radiator wing, on the sun-side of the ship. The glycol lines run through a manifold bolted to the spine, connecting to the wing panels via a flanged joint. The seal has degraded. It is not a crack, but a fatigue failure. The metal has tired, and it is weeping through the microscopic gaps in the seal."

He pointed to the schematic on the wall, a faded diagram of the spine and wings that looked like a skeleton picked clean. "To fix it, you must replace the seal, or the whole joint. You cannot do that from inside. The access hatch is too small for a person, and the mechanism is locked from the outside. So you have to go out there. Into the vacuum."

Kess felt a chill that had nothing to do with the ambient temperature in the pump house, a cold that settled in the marrow of her bones and refused to leave. "An EVA," she said. "A full spacewalk."

"Exactly," Voss said. "And it is not just a walk. It is a walk in a narrow window. The ship’s attitude must position the wing in shadow, so the thermal load on the joint is low enough that the heat does not warp the metal while you are working. That window happens only once every few months. And it is tight. Very tight."

He paused, and his voice lost its professional edge, softening into something more human and more tired. "The last team that went out for a similar repair, eight years ago, lost a man. Not his life. His career. His left hand. He is alive, but he cannot work anymore. He retired. Since then, no one has gone out. Because the risk is too high. Because the Council is afraid. Because they think that if we send someone out and something goes wrong, they will be the ones to explain it."

Lio’s face had gone pale, the color draining from his cheeks like water from a basin. He looked at Kess, and in his eyes she saw the same apprehension gripping her own chest, a fear of the void, of the thin tethers, of the cold.

"So we cannot fix it?" Kess asked, her voice sounding smaller than she intended.

"We can," Voss said. "But we have to be perfect. And we have to be fast. And we have to be brave. And we have to be young. Because I am not young anymore. And I am not brave enough to risk my life for a leak that I know I should have fixed years ago."
pages.image: Chief Voss points to a schematic diagram on the wall, showing the ship's spine and radiator wing; Kess and Lio look at the diagram with apprehension, the mood tense and serious, the industrial lighting casting sharp shadows on their faces.

pages.text:
"Why does no one know?" Kess asked. Her voice was quiet, yet it sliced through the rhythmic thrum of the coolant pumps with a sharpness that seemed to still the air in the gallery. "Why do we not have a public alert, or even a genuine discussion?"

Voss looked at her, and for a moment she suspected he might be angry, but his expression was instead one of profound, exhausted weariness. He reached up and rubbed his eyes, a gesture that appeared to drain the last of his strength from his shoulders.

"Directive Nine," he said, his tone flat and factual. "It states that Level-Four system faults cannot be disclosed to the general population without Council authorization. The Council has not authorized it. They are afraid. They believe that the truth is heavier for the people to carry than the leak itself. They think that if everyone knows the ship is slowly dying, they will panic, stop working, or simply stop believing that it can be fixed."

"That’s not true," Pim said. He stood close to Kess, his small hands clenched tight at his sides where the fabric of his red hooded sweatshirt pulled taut. "We know. We know about the leak and the margin. We’re not panicking. We’re trying to fix it."

Voss looked at the boy, and a small, sad smile touched his lips. "Yes. You are. And that is why you are annoying. And that is why I like you. And that is why I am telling you this."

He stood up, his joints creaking in protest against the sudden weight. "I have been waiting eleven years for someone to ask the right question. Not 'what is the number?' but 'why is it hidden?' You asked it. Now you know. And now you have a choice. You can forget it. You can go back to your orchard, your apples, and your little drone. Or you can help me fix this. And you can help me tell the truth."

Kess looked at Lio, who was staring at the drone on the workbench. The orange glow on its screen pulsed, steady and sure against the dim workshop light.

"We have twenty-six days," Kess said. "Landing Day is in twenty-six days. And the vote is on Landing Day."

Voss nodded slowly. "Then I suggest you do not waste any of them being polite."
pages.image: Kess stands facing Chief Voss in the pump house, her expression determined; Pim stands beside her, looking up with a fierce, questioning gaze; the drone on the bench glows softly, the scene charged with resolve and urgency.

pages.text:
The silence that followed was not empty; it was full, dense with the gravity of the choice hanging in the air. Kess felt the hum of the pumps in her bones, a steady, rhythmic vibration that seemed to sync with her own heartbeat. She looked at Voss, at the tired lines in his face, at the grease stains on his coverall that mapped the years of his work.

"I’m in," she said.

Lio stepped forward, his voice steady. "I’m in."

Pim looked up at them, his yellow hair-ties bouncing slightly. "I’m in," he said. "I have questions. Lots of questions. But I’m in."

Voss looked at them, and for a long moment, he smiled. It was not a big smile; it was small, quiet, and a little bit crooked, but it was real.

"Good," he said. "Then we have work to do. And we have a lot of it. And we have to do it fast. Because the ship is not going to wait for us. And the truth is not going to wait for us either."

He picked up the wrench from the bench and held it out to Kess. "Start here," he said. "Find the joint. Map the leak. And then we will plan. But we will plan with our heads, not our hearts. Because the heart is a good thing, but the head is the only thing that can save us."

Kess took the wrench. It was heavy, cold, and solid. It felt right in her hand, like a tool that had been waiting for her. She looked at Lio, and he nodded, a small, silent promise passing between them. They had a plan. They had a tool. They had each other. And they had twenty-six days.

The grow-lights hummed their low, constant note, casting long shadows across the metal floor. The ship turned, steady and sure, carrying them all toward a future that they were building, one careful step at a time. And in the pump house, the drone sat, ready to fly.
